title: Container networking
description: Understand Docker's networking models, bridge and host networks, network isolation, and how to configure secure container communication in production.

data.text: Docker networking controls which containers can talk to each other, how they discover each other, and how traffic flows between containers and the outside world. A misconfigured network can expose internal services to the internet or allow a compromised container to reach systems it should never touch.

When you install Docker, it creates three networks automatically: `bridge`, `host`, and `none`. If you do not specify a network when you start a container, Docker connects it to the default `bridge` network. Every container on the same user-defined bridge network can communicate with every other container on that network by name.

data.title: Built-in networks are for Docker's internal use
data.text: Do not attach production containers directly to the built-in `bridge` network. Create a user-defined bridge network for your application so containers can resolve each other by name and are isolated from unrelated containers.
Network drivers and their security properties

rows: All containers on the same bridge can reach each other
Container shares the host network stack; no network isolation
Encrypted traffic between swarm nodes with VXLAN
Container gets its own MAC and IP on the LAN

data.text: A typical three-tier application has a frontend, an API, and a database. Each tier should live on its own Docker network. The frontend needs to reach the API. The API needs to reach the database. The frontend should never reach the database directly.

data.title: Isolated tier networks with Docker Compose
data.content: This Compose file creates separate networks for each tier. Containers can only communicate along the paths you explicitly allow.
data.code:
services:
  frontend:
    image: myapp-frontend
    networks:
      - public
      - backend
  api:
    image: myapp-api
    networks:
      - backend
      - data
  database:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    networks:
      - data

networks:
  public:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true
  data:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true

data.title: The host network is almost never what you want
data.text: `network_mode: host` removes all network isolation. The container shares the host's IP addresses, ports, and firewall rules. Use it only for high-performance monitoring agents or when a specific application cannot operate inside a network namespace.

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile is documentation. It does not open any ports. `docker run -p` or the `ports` section in Compose is what actually publishes container ports to the host. Only publish the ports that external systems need. Do not publish database ports to the host network.

data.title: Port publishing rules of thumb
items: Bind to `127.0.0.1` on the host when only the host or a reverse proxy needs access: `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:3000`
Use Compose `expose` for service-to-service communication without host publishing
Reserve `ports` for services that must be reachable from outside the Docker host

data.text: Docker network isolation is not a complete security boundary. A root user inside a container can manipulate network namespaces. Treat Docker networking as one layer of defense and enforce host-level firewall rules, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, or service mesh policies for sensitive workloads.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: User-defined bridge networks provide name-based discovery and basic isolation
Separate application tiers onto separate networks to limit blast radius
Avoid the host network driver except for narrow use cases
Bind published ports to localhost when external access is not required
Complement Docker networking with host firewalls and, in Kubernetes, NetworkPolicy
data.takeaway: Good container networking is about least privilege: every container should be able to reach only what it truly needs.
